name: Koshi Tappu
image_query: Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve wetland birds
tagline: Wild water buffalo and winter birds on the Koshi floodplain
meta_description: Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve: Nepal's first Ramsar site, home of its last wild water buffalo (arna), winter waterbirds, river boats and the Koshi Barrage.
summary: Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve protects about 176 square kilometres of reed beds, grassland and river channels on the Koshi floodplain in eastern Nepal. It shelters the country's last wild water buffalo, or arna, and is one of Nepal's richest places for waterbirds. Visit for two nights, November to March, flying into Biratnagar.
intro: In eastern Nepal the Sapta Koshi, the country's largest river, leaves the hills and spreads across a wide plain before crossing into Bihar. Just above the Koshi Barrage, its floodplain becomes a maze of channels, sandbanks, marsh and tall grass at 75 to 81 metres above sea level. This is Koshi Tappu, set up as a wildlife reserve in 1976. Villages and farmland surround the reserve on all sides.

The reserve was created mainly to protect the arna, the wild water buffalo, whose last population in Nepal lives here. Bigger and wilder-looking than domestic buffalo, with huge swept-back horns, arna graze the grasslands at dawn and dusk. The reserve also holds gharial and mugger crocodiles, river dolphins in the Koshi, and more than 200 species of fish. Smooth-coated otters, hog deer and golden jackals also live here.

But most visitors come for birds. In winter the channels and marshes fill with ducks, geese, storks, herons, cranes and raptors, and the grassland hides rare residents such as the swamp francolin. In December 1987 Koshi Tappu became Nepal's first Ramsar wetland. Fly to Biratnagar, drive about 1.5 to 2 hours, and spend two nights in a camp near the reserve's edge. Plan for early starts; the first hours of light are the best.

story.title: A river that moves, a buffalo that stayed
paras: The Koshi is famous for changing course. Carrying silt from Everest, Makalu and Kanchenjunga, it has shifted its bed across the plain many times, earning the name 'Sorrow of Bihar' for the floods it sends downstream. In the 1950s Nepal and India agreed to tame it, and between 1958 and 1962 the Koshi Barrage was built near the border, with 56 gates. The river still carries so much sediment that its channels keep shifting from year to year.

Above the barrage the river still spreads and floods each monsoon, renewing grassland and wetland. That is the habitat the arna needs. By the 1970s hunting, grazing and farming had reduced Nepal's wild water buffalo to a single small herd, and in 1976 the government set up Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve to save it. In 1987 the reserve was listed under the Ramsar Convention, and in 2005 it was named an Important Bird Area together with the barrage. It remains the arna's only home in Nepal.

Living beside the reserve is not easy. Wild buffalo and boar raid crops, domestic cattle graze inside, and in August 2008 the Koshi broke its eastern embankment north of the barrage, flooding farmland and displacing tens of thousands of people in Nepal and millions in Bihar. The reserve and its neighbours are still finding a balance between people, river and wildlife. Visitors who come with local guides and stay in local camps help show that the wetland is worth more alive than drained.

people: Villages around Koshi Tappu are home to Tharu families, including Kochila Tharu, Maithili-speaking Madhesi communities, and fishing communities such as the Mallah and Musahar, who have long worked the Koshi's channels with nets and small boats. Hill settlers farm on higher ground. People grow rice, jute, wheat and lentils and graze cattle, and some work as boatmen and bird guides.

untold.fact: Koshi Tappu was designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in December 1987, making it Nepal's first Ramsar site.
untold.source: Wikipedia: Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve; Ramsar Sites Information Service

untold.fact: The reserve was established in 1976 and holds Nepal's last remaining population of wild water buffalo, Bubalus arnee, known locally as arna.

Grassland covers about 68 per cent of the reserve and forest only about 6 per cent; around 200 fish species have been recorded in its waters, and the Ganges river dolphin has been sighted in the Koshi.

local_words.meaning: Island; the reserve is named for the river islands of the Koshi

taste.name: Koshi fish curry
taste.text: Fish from the Koshi is cooked in mustard oil with turmeric, chilli and tomato and eaten with rice. Riverside restaurants near the Koshi Barrage are known for it, and camps near the reserve serve it when the catch is fresh. Ask for small river fish fried crisp as a side.

highlights.title: Arna, the wild water buffalo
highlights.text: Nepal's only wild water buffalo graze the reserve's grasslands, with massive swept-back horns that can span more than a metre. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times to see a herd. Watch from a safe distance.

highlights.title: Winter waterbirds
highlights.text: From November to March the channels and marshes fill with ducks, geese, storks, herons, ibises and raptors. Koshi Tappu and the barrage are among Nepal's top birding sites. Bring binoculars and warm layers.

highlights.title: Boat trips on the Koshi
highlights.text: Local boatmen take visitors along the channels for close views of waterbirds, crocodiles and, with luck, Ganges river dolphins surfacing in the main river. Morning trips give the softest light and calmest water.

highlights.title: The Koshi Barrage
highlights.text: Built between 1958 and 1962 with 56 gates, the barrage spans the Koshi near the border. Birds gather on the water above it, and riverside eateries nearby serve fresh fish. Carry your passport near the border.

highlights.title: Grassland specialists
highlights.text: The tall grass hides rare birds such as the swamp francolin, as well as hog deer and wild boar. Walks along the embankment at dawn give the best chances. Go with a bird guide who knows the calls.

how_to_reach.text: Fly from Kathmandu to Biratnagar (BIR), about 35 to 40 minutes, then drive about 1.5 to 2 hours west to the reserve. Rajbiraj airport, about 26 km from the barrage, also has flights from Kathmandu. Check current status before you travel.

From Kathmandu it is about 400 km and 10 to 12 hours via the BP Highway and East-West Highway. From Janakpur allow 4 to 5 hours east along the East-West Highway. Night buses run from Kathmandu to Itahari and Biratnagar.

where_to_stay: A small number of tented camps and lodges operate near the reserve's eastern edge, run by birding operators with their own guides and boats; standards are simple but comfortable, and some close in the monsoon. Itahari and Biratnagar, 1 to 2 hours away, have city hotels. For serious birding, stay at a camp near the reserve so you are in the field at dawn. Book ahead for December to February.
tips: Go from November to March for the best birding; December to February is peak season for migrants.
Bring binoculars, a spotting scope if you have one, and a bird guide or app for South Asia.
Pack warm layers for foggy winter mornings on the water.
Keep well back from wild buffalo; they can be aggressive, especially bulls and mothers with calves.
Check current reserve fees and access rules, which change; the 2023 guide rule for national parks may apply.

experiences.title: Boat birding on the Koshi channels
experiences.summary: Glide along the Koshi's channels with a local boatman and a bird guide, close to ducks, storks, herons and cormorants, with crocodiles on the banks and the chance of river dolphins in the main stream.
body: Boat trips start soon after dawn, when mist sits on the water and birds are most active. Local boatmen pole or paddle flat-bottomed boats through the quieter side channels, getting closer to birds than you can on foot. Your bird guide calls out species as they appear. Trips last two to three hours, depending on the route and water level.

In winter expect large flocks of ducks, including ruddy shelducks, gadwall and pintails, alongside cormorants, egrets, herons, storks and ibises. Raptors such as ospreys and marsh harriers patrol overhead. Mugger crocodiles and occasionally gharials bask on sandbanks. Bar-headed geese and other migrants appear in the coldest months, and a large flock taking off is a sound you remember.

In the main river, watch for the rolling back of a Ganges river dolphin surfacing to breathe. Sightings are rare but possible. Wear warm layers in December and January, carry binoculars and a camera with a long lens, and keep still in the boat. Your guide can tell you which channels have had recent dolphin sightings.

faqs.q: What birds can I see at Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: In winter, large flocks of ducks and geese, storks, herons, egrets, ibises, cormorants and raptors such as ospreys and harriers. Grassland residents include the swamp francolin. Koshi Tappu and the Koshi Barrage together are listed as an Important Bird Area and are among Nepal's best birding sites.

faqs.q: Are there dolphins at Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: The Ganges river dolphin has been sighted in the Koshi River. It is endangered and rarely seen, surfacing briefly to breathe. Boat trips on the main river give the best chance. Ask your guide about recent sightings, and be patient.

faqs.q: Is the Koshi boat trip safe?
faqs.a: Yes, with experienced local boatmen in the dry season, when the water is calm. Wear a life jacket if offered, sit still and do not trail hands in the water, as crocodiles live in the river. Boat trips do not run in the monsoon, when the river is high and dangerous.

experiences.title: Searching for arna, the wild buffalo
experiences.summary: Go out with a reserve guide at dawn or dusk to find herds of arna, Nepal's last wild water buffalo, grazing the grasslands of Koshi Tappu, with hog deer, wild boar and grassland birds along the way.
body: The arna is the reason Koshi Tappu exists. Wild water buffalo are larger and leaner than their domestic cousins, with huge, wide horns that sweep back in a crescent. Nepal's only population lives here, in the grasslands and marshes between the Koshi's channels. Their horns are among the largest of any living wild cattle.

Your guide leads you by jeep or on foot along the embankments and grassland edges in the first and last hours of light, when the buffalo leave cover to graze. Herds can be shy or bold. Bulls and mothers with calves may charge if approached, so keep a safe distance and follow your guide. Patience matters more than speed.

Along the way look for hog deer, wild boar, golden jackals and smooth-coated otters, and grassland birds such as the swamp francolin, whose loud calls carry across the reeds. Wear neutral colours, bring binoculars and plenty of water. Afternoon outings end at dusk, when herds are active. Your guide carries the permits.

faqs.q: What is an arna?
faqs.a: Arna is the Nepali name for the wild water buffalo, Bubalus arnee, an endangered species and the wild ancestor of domestic buffalo. In Nepal it survives only in Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve, which was established in 1976 largely to protect it.

faqs.q: How can I tell a wild water buffalo from a domestic one?
faqs.a: Wild buffalo are generally larger and leaner, with longer legs and much bigger horns that sweep wide and back. Domestic buffalo also graze in and around the reserve, and the two sometimes mix, which is a conservation concern. Your guide will help you tell them apart.

faqs.q: Are wild water buffalo dangerous?
faqs.a: They can be. Bulls and mothers with calves may charge if they feel threatened. Always keep a safe distance, stay with your guide, and never approach on foot for photographs. Viewing from a jeep or embankment is safest.

experiences.title: Dawn walk on the Koshi embankment
experiences.summary: Walk the raised embankments at the edge of the reserve as the sun rises over marsh and grass, listening for swamp francolins, watching harriers quarter the reeds and scanning the wetlands for cranes, storks and ducks.
body: The embankments built to contain the Koshi now make perfect walking paths. Raised above the floodplain, they give long views over marshes, pools and grassland. At dawn mist drifts across the reeds, and birds call from every direction. They are the easiest way to see the reserve on foot, with long views and firm ground.

Listen for the loud, repeated call of the swamp francolin, a grassland bird with a small and declining range. Marsh harriers quarter low over the reeds, while storks, herons and egrets stand in shallow water. In winter, flocks of ducks lift off the pools as the light grows. Kingfishers, bee-eaters and prinias are common along the way.

Walks are easy and flat. Go with a bird guide who knows the best stretches and the latest sightings. Wear warm layers in winter and waterproof shoes if the ground is wet. Combine with a boat trip later in the morning. Walks last two to three hours and end before the day warms up.

faqs.q: What is the swamp francolin?
faqs.a: The swamp francolin is a ground-dwelling bird of tall wet grasslands in the Terai and northern India. It is listed as vulnerable because its habitat has largely been converted to farmland. Koshi Tappu is one of the best places in Nepal to hear and see it, especially at dawn.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for walks at Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: Yes, we recommend a licensed guide for any walk in or near the reserve. Wild buffalo and boar can be dangerous, and a bird guide finds and identifies far more species. Rules on guides in protected areas can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time for birding at Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: November to March, with December to February the peak for migrant waterbirds. Early mornings are best. Spring brings breeding residents and some passage migrants. The monsoon, from June to September, floods much of the area and is not suitable for visits.

experiences.title: Koshi Barrage and a riverside fish lunch
experiences.summary: Visit the Koshi Barrage, built between 1958 and 1962 with 56 gates, watch birds on the water above it, then eat fresh Koshi fish at one of the riverside eateries that draw families from across the region.
body: The Koshi Barrage spans the river near the India border, carrying road traffic between Madhesh and Koshi provinces. It was built under an agreement between Nepal and India signed in 1954 to control floods and supply irrigation. Its 56 gates hold back the water into a wide, calm stretch above. Trucks, buses and bicycles cross it all day.

That calm water is a magnet for birds in winter: ducks, gulls, terns, cormorants and herons gather in large numbers, and birders scan from the barrage itself. The Ganges river dolphin has been seen in the river here too. Bring binoculars and scan the open water and sandbars; gulls and terns are easiest to see in winter.

Then comes lunch. Simple riverside eateries near the barrage are known across eastern Nepal for fresh fish, fried crisp or cooked in a mustard-oil curry and served with rice. Ask your guide for a busy place, choose fish cooked fresh and enjoy it looking over the river. Afterwards, the reserve is a short drive north for an afternoon walk or boat trip.

faqs.q: What is the Koshi Barrage?
faqs.a: The Koshi Barrage is a sluice across the Koshi River near the Nepal–India border, built between 1958 and 1962 under an agreement signed in 1954. It has 56 gates and carries road traffic between Madhesh and Koshi provinces. Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve lies a few kilometres upstream.

faqs.q: Can I visit the Koshi Barrage as a tourist?
faqs.a: Yes, the barrage is on a public road and many Nepali families visit it for the views and fish restaurants. Photography rules near the structure may apply, so follow signs and ask your guide. Carry your passport, as you are close to the India border.

faqs.q: What kind of fish is served at the Koshi Barrage?
faqs.a: Local river fish caught in the Koshi and nearby ponds, cooked fried or in a mustard-oil curry with rice. Species vary by season and catch. Choose freshly cooked fish from busy places, and ask about bones before you start if you are eating with children.

faqs.q: Where is Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve?
faqs.a: Koshi Tappu lies in eastern Nepal on the floodplain of the Sapta Koshi River, in Sunsari, Saptari and Udayapur districts, a few kilometres upstream of the Koshi Barrage. The nearest airport is Biratnagar, about 1.5 to 2 hours by road; Rajbiraj airport is also close to the barrage.

faqs.q: What is Koshi Tappu famous for?
faqs.a: Koshi Tappu is famous for Nepal's last population of wild water buffalo, the arna, and for outstanding birdlife, especially winter waterbirds. It was Nepal's first Ramsar wetland, listed in December 1987, and is an Important Bird Area together with the Koshi Barrage.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: November to March, when migrant waterbirds are present and the weather is cool and dry. December to February is the peak birding season. The monsoon, from June to September, floods much of the area, and many camps close. Spring is hot but still good for resident birds.

faqs.q: How do I get to Koshi Tappu from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly from Kathmandu to Biratnagar in about 35 to 40 minutes and drive about 1.5 to 2 hours. By road it is about 400 km and 10 to 12 hours via the BP Highway and East-West Highway. Many travellers combine Koshi Tappu with Janakpur, 4 to 5 hours to the west.

faqs.q: How many days do I need at Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: Two nights is ideal: one full day for boat trips, embankment walks and searching for wild buffalo, with dawn and dusk sessions. Keen birders often stay three or four nights to cover more habitats and the barrage. Start at first light each day.

faqs.q: Where can I stay at Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: A small number of tented camps and lodges operate near the reserve's eastern edge, run by birding operators with their own guides and boats. Itahari and Biratnagar have city hotels 1 to 2 hours away. Camps near the reserve are best for dawn birding; book ahead for winter.

faqs.q: Is Koshi Tappu good for non-birders?
faqs.a: It can be, if you enjoy quiet landscapes, boat trips and village life, and want to see the wild water buffalo. But it does not have Chitwan's rhinos and big predators. Non-birders on a short trip usually prefer Chitwan; Koshi Tappu suits nature lovers with time.

faqs.q: Is Koshi Tappu now a national park?
faqs.a: Koshi Tappu has long been managed as a wildlife reserve, and there have been discussions about changing its status. Names, fees and rules for protected areas in Nepal do change, so check current status before you travel and confirm entry fees with your operator.

faqs.q: Can I see wild water buffalo for sure at Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: Sightings are likely but not guaranteed. Herds graze the grasslands in the early morning and late afternoon, and a good guide knows where they have been seen recently. Dense grass and floods can hide them. Two days on site improves your chances.
